speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: asked the Minister for Health in light of network hardware issues affecting the IT systems of public healthcare institutions on 27 August 2022 (a) how many institutions, apps and IT-dependent services are affected respectively; (b) how many patients are existing inpatients, patients admitted that day and outpatients scheduled to be seen that day respectively; (c) how many of such patients have experienced diversion or delayed care provision; and (d) how are the affected patients and healthcare workers supported.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There was a related outage that occurred in the morning of 5 September 2022, which I will also address.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: From 7.00 am on 27 August 2022, the public healthcare monitoring systems detected IT network connectivity failures.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The faults were rectified and the systems were restored by 10.45 am on the same day.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Seventeen public healthcare institutions, including the acute hospitals, community hospitals and specialist outpatient clinics and all the polyclinics, were also affected.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: On 5 September, at 10.00 am, another fault occurred in the IT infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Some functionality was restored from 1.00 pm on the same day and full functionality was restored by 6.00 pm the next day.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This outage affected eight public healthcare institutions and two out of three polyclinic groups.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Due to the nature of this outage, the time to recovery of the system was longer.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Hence, operations and services were switched to their back-up infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Both incidents caused a significant impact on operations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: On both 27 August and 5 September, our affected public healthcare institutions activated their downtime procedures and business continuity plans to keep operations running using alternative systems and, in some cases, manual documentation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These business continuity plans are exercised regularly and staff were able to switch processes to sustain operations during the outage.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But they had to work doubly hard to keep healthcare operations running smoothly.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There were delays in dispensing medications to patients.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Fortunately, there was no compromise to urgent care services across the institutions during the IT disruptions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Nobody was turned away from the emergency departments or denied urgent care.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are investigating the incidents with the manufacturer of the IT hardware to rectify any weaknesses in the system.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is what we have found out so far.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Public healthcare IT infrastructure is housed in more than one data centre for resilience and redundancy.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: At each data centre, there are a few firewall zones.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Each firewall zone consists of multiple nodes, these are hardware devices which operate in tandem, so if one fails, the load of data traffic is managed by the other nodes in the cluster, so that service operation is uninterrupted.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This system had generally been working well until the recent outages.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: On 25 August, two days before the incident that we are describing here, on 25 August, a node failed and the system resilience features kicked in and services were maintained.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The same thing happened on the 26 August, when another node failed and the systems and services continued functioning.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: On 27 August, when the engineers tried to restore the two failed nodes, under the supervision of the manufacturer and following the manufacturer's procedures, which had been successfully used in the past, the operation failed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is this failed operation that caused the cluster of firewall nodes to malfunction and subsequently caused the outage.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The engineers worked to reset the systems to the prior state without the function of the two affected nodes and service was progressively restored.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The failure of the nodes was caused by bugs in the firmware of the devices.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They have since been identified by the manufacturer, CISCO, and the devices have been patched.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The outage on 5 September was caused by the simultaneous failure of two further nodes, again from the same manufacturer and of the same model.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The way in which this failure on 5 September occurred, was noted to be different from the previous incident, it was assessed that it would take longer to restore operations, and hence, the decision was made to switch operations to the back-up systems.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The root cause of why these two nodes failed is still under investigation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There was a suggestion in one of questions from Members that the failures may be due to the lack of manpower at IHiS.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They have a lot to do and will always welcome more manpower, but a lack of manpower was not the cause of these failures.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our cybersecurity specialists are monitoring our network and systems for threats in our public healthcare network at all times.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: When the network problems occurred, IHiS initiated an investigation and also alerted the Cyber Security Agency.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Based on the investigations thus far, there are no indications of security compromise to the affected systems.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: All the firewall hardware involved in the incidents are from the same established device manufacturer.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Fixes for some of the issues have been made available and have been deployed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For the others we continue to work with the manufacturer.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In the meantime, we have increased capacity in the network for more operational buffer to increase resilience.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will continue to review our system design and architecture, and invest in capabilities and readiness to reduce disruptions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Disruptions like this can occur again in the future and we continue to have at the ready back-up systems, downtime procedures and manual processes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Once again, Mr Speaker, allow me to express my thanks to all the personnel of our public healthcare system who kept our patients safe and the services running and for the members of the public who were involved and affected during these days for their patience and understanding as we tried to cope and mitigate the circumstances as best we could.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I had Clementi residents contacting me – some were affected and saw how hard it was on the doctors and nurses, who nevertheless rose to the occasion and made efforts to help despite the outage.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some healthcare workers living in Clementi also contacted me and were concerned about the reliability of the system.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have the following supplementary questions for MOH.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: First, how do we benchmark our systems' reliability and usability?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Do we take reference from best-in-class examples elsewhere?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Do we know whether this hardware item has given similar issues elsewhere in the world?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If not, what is being done to look for other as yet, undiscovered potential vulnerabilities?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: His first question was about the benchmarking of reliability and usability.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The second question was about the hardware, were there similar issues and what are we doing to look at vulnerabilities, and I think, other vulnerabilities with similar hardware.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The hardware that was involved is used in other parts of Government systems but in relatively limited numbers and they are configured differently.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And this is partly because the way in which the Government requires its data flow and its inter-operability, its system architecture, is different from the requirements of the healthcare space.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And so, the specific configurations for this type of hardware in the rest of the Government, is not present.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But nevertheless, we are working together, the various agencies that are involved in public sector technology – Cyber Security Agency, GovTech, IHiS and others – share information and are looking to scan across the various infrastructure that we have to check on these possibilities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Also, is there training given to these frontline staff about what to do and what the business continuity plans (BCPs) were and also do these plans need to be updated after what happened in the last two instances?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The support for frontline staff, indeed, the support from MOH and IHiS is largely around the communication and providing clear information about what has happened, what are the expected steps taken to restore functionality and how much time will be required.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Because, the next set of decisions, which BCPs and processes to implement are done at an operational level, depending on the needs of each team.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, from IHiS and MOH, a lot of the support is around communication.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Within the healthcare ecosystem and the clusters, clearly, they mobilised staff, they mobilised the senior staff and the junior staff, everybody had their hands on deck to cope and deal with the outages as well as the extra processes required for the outages.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And that includes overtime for some staff, having to work extra hours, and then, consequently, overtime claims as a result of that.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And so, the entire team mobilises together to support each other and we provide as much support as we can to help them through this difficult time.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They are part of standard training for all the healthcare workers that are in our public healthcare sector and the training is updated on a regular basis.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is not something that is standardised in every team and in every unit across the healthcare ecosystem because these are peculiar to the operations and flows within each clinical team.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And so, you have standards that are set broadly, expectations that are set, guidance that are set.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But then each team will develop the granularity of their business continuity plans and these are then drilled as well.
